entry.title: The Axioms of Set Theory
entry.content:
Ask a room full of students what the most fundamental thing in mathematics is and most of them will say numbers. Fair enough. We all start learning mathematics by counting. Yet a vast majority of mathematics can be built directly out of something even more primitive: sets. Over this series we will actually do it, constructing the natural numbers out of nothing but sets (and, as we will see, quite literally out of nothing).

This post is the first in a series on elementary set theory, adapted from my textbook in progress. Our goal is to get a working introduction to sets, and then to peel back a few layers and look at their foundational nature. The hope is that we come away knowing not only how to use and play with sets, but also how they shape the very fabric of modern mathematics.

Sets and Subsets

Definition 2.1. A set is a well-definedWhat it means for a set to be well-defined is exactly what the axioms of set theory, further down this post, are for. collection of distinct elements.

Notation first, because we are going to use a lot of it.

Remark 2.1. A few comments on notation before we proceed.

  1. A set $X$ can oftenThere are sets for which a roster is not possible, such as the real numbers. One of the axioms below gives us a more general way to specify sets. be specified by a roster or list of its elements enclosed within curly braces, i.e., $X := \lbrace \dots brace$, where the “$\dots$” are placeholders for the elements of $X$.
  2. If $x$ is an element of the set $X$, we write $x \in X$. We read this as “$x$ is in $X$” or “$x$ belongs to $X$”.
  3. If $x$ is not an element of the set $X$, we write $x otin X$. We read this as “$x$ is not in $X$” or “$x$ does not belong to $X$”.

Example 2.1. $X := \lbrace 1, 2, 3 brace$ is a set, and $2 \in X$, but $5 otin X$.

Example 2.2. $\mathbb{Z} := \lbrace \dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots brace$ is the set of integers, and $-7 \in \mathbb{Z}$, but $0.5 otin \mathbb{Z}$.

Once we have sets, the most basic question we can ask about two of them is whether one sits inside the other.

Definition 2.2. A set $A$ is called a subset of a set $B$ if and only if $ orall a : (a \in A \implies a \in B)$, and we write $A \subseteq B$. The set $B$ is then called a superset of $A$, written $B \supseteq A$. When this is not the case, we write $A ot\subseteq B$ and $B ot\supseteq A$.

In plain English: every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$.

Example 2.3. Let $A := \lbrace 1, 2, 3 brace$ and $B := \lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 brace$. Then $A \subseteq B$, but $C := \lbrace 5, 6 brace ot\subseteq B$.

The next example trips up a surprising number of people, so read it slowly.

Example 2.4. Let $A := \lbrace 1, \lbrace 2, 3 brace brace$. Then $B := \lbrace 2, 3 brace \in A$, but $B ot\subseteq A$, since $2 \in B$ while $2 otin A$. However, the set $\lbrace B brace \subseteq A$. Furthermore, $\lbrace 2 brace ot\subseteq A$, and $2 otin A$ either, despite $2 \in B$ and $B \in A$. Being an element of an element does not make you an element.

Example 2.5. The set of natural numbers is a subset of the set of integers, which is in turn a subset of the set of rational numbers, i.e., $\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$.

Theorem 2.1. Every set is a subset of itself.

Proof

We will prove this by contradiction. Let $A$ be a set with $A ot\subseteq A$. ThenHere we use that $P \implies Q$ is logically equivalent to $ eg P \lor Q$, so its negation is $P \land eg Q$. it is not the case that $ orall a : (a \in A \implies a \in A)$, so $\exists a : (a \in A \land a otin A)$, which is a contradiction. Thus $A \subseteq A$. $\square$

Definition 2.3. Two sets are disjoint when they share no common elements.

Example 2.6. The set $\lbrace 1, 2 brace$ is disjoint from $\lbrace 3, 4 brace$ but not from $\lbrace 1, 3 brace$.

Example 2.7. The set of rational numbers and the set of irrational numbers are disjoint.

So far, so harmless. Collect some things in curly braces, check what is inside what. What could possibly go wrong?

Axioms of Set Theory

Historically, set theory was not developed as a consistent axiomatic system. It was developed intuitively, in simple language, and simple language turned out to be a trap. It led to a bunch of paradoxes, which in turn led to what is now called the foundational crisis in mathematics. Let’s look at the most famous one.

Theorem 2.2 (Russell). There is no set of all sets that are not members of themselves.This is the much-famed Russell's paradox. Bertrand Russell was an influential mathematician and philosopher whose contributions greatly shaped the foundations of mathematics.

Proof

We will prove this by contradiction. Suppose such a set $R$ exists, i.e., the elements $X \in R$ are exactly the sets with $X otin X$. Now ask whether $R$ is a member of itself. If $R \in R$, then $R$ fails the condition for membership, so $R otin R$. If $R otin R$, then $R$ satisfies the condition, so $R \in R$. Either way we have a contradiction, so no such set $R$ exists. $\square$

Russell came across this in 1901 and published it in The Principles of Mathematics. Before you dismiss it as a cute word game, notice what actually went wrong. We wrote down a perfectly sensible-sounding property, “is not a member of itself”, and assumed that the collection of everything with that property is a set. The naïve, vanilla version of set theory does nothing to stop us from doing that, because it never properly specifies what can and cannot be a set. And Russell’s is far from the only paradox of this kind.

So it falls upon us to write down axioms that make sets well-defined. The first axiomatisation was given by Ernst Zermelo in 1908. Abraham Fraenkel’s improvements in 1922 led to what we now call Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory, or ZF. Add the axiom of choice and you get ZFC.

Definition 2.4. For a set to be well-defined, it must satisfy the ZFC axioms below.

(Null Set) There exists a set with no elements, called the null setAlso known as the empty set. and denoted by $\varnothing$.

(Extension) Two sets are equal if and only if they have the same elements.

(Foundation) Every non-empty set $S$ contains an element that is disjoint from $S$.If this one looks strange, you are paying attention. The remarks after this list explain it.

(Specification) For any predicate $P$ and any set $S$, the elements $x \in S$ satisfyingTechnically this is an axiom schema, because it is one axiom for every predicate $P$. $P(x)$ form a set, denoted byThis is called set-builder notation. $\lbrace x \in S : P(x) brace$.

(Pairing) For any two sets $A$ and $B$, there exists a set that contains $A$ and $B$.

(Union) For any set $S$, there exists a set containing every element of every $x \in S$.

(Power Set) For any set $S$, there exists a set of all subsets of $S$, called the power set of $S$ and denoted by $\mathcal{P}(S)$.

(Replacement) The imageImages will be discussed properly when we get to relations and functions. of a set under any definable mapping is also a set.

(Infinity) There exists at least one set containing infinitely many elements.

(Choice) For any set $S$ of non-empty sets, there exists a choice functionThis is a can of worms that we will not open any further, but we will be using it implicitly in a bunch of places. that assigns to each $X \in S$ an element of $X$ itself.

Remark 2.2. The axiom of foundation may seem strange at first glance, especially when we consider a set like $\lbrace 1, 2, 3 brace$. What does it even mean for a number to be disjoint from a set? To answer this, we must first construct numbers using sets and say exactly what they are. We will do this in the post on inductive sets, two posts from now.

Remark 2.3. The axiom of foundationAlso known as the axiom of regularity, in the sense that it regulates set membership. rules out exactly the kind of self-membership that the Russell set $R$ of Theorem 2.2 trips over. In Theorem 2.6, in the next post, we show that it forbids self-membership ($x \in x$), membership loops ($x \in y \in x$) and infinite descending chains of membership ($\dots \in x_n \in \dots \in x_1 \in x_0$).

Remark 2.4. The axiom of specificationAlso known as the axiom of restricted comprehension. It is restricted in the sense that the elements must be comprehended from an existing set and cannot simply be anything. gives us the very useful set-builder notation. We read $S := \lbrace x \in A : P(x) brace$ in plain English as:

$S$ is defined to be ($S :=$) the set of all ($\lbrace \dots brace$) elements $x$ in the set $A$ ($x \in A$) such that ($:$) $P(x)$ is true.

This notation is very helpful when dealing with large sets. Notice also what it does not let us do: we can only carve elements out of a set $A$ we already have. We cannot simply declare “the set of everything with property $P$”, which is precisely the move that landed us in Russell’s paradox.

Example 2.8. $S := \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 2 \mid n brace$ is read as “$S$ is defined to be the set of all elements $n$ in the set of integers such that $2$ divides $n$”. As a roster, $S = \lbrace \dots, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, \dots brace$.

With the axiom of extension in hand, we can sharpen our notion of a subset.

Definition 2.5. A subset $A$ of a set $B$, i.e., $A \subseteq B$, is called a proper subset$B$ is then a proper superset of $A$, but this terminology is rarely used. when $A eq B$. This is denoted by $A \subset B$ or sometimes $A \subsetneq B$. A subset that is not proper is called an improper subset.

Fair warning: plenty of books use $\subset$ to mean $\subseteq$. Always check a book’s conventions before trusting its symbols.

Theorem 2.3. Every set has a unique improper subset, namely the set itself.

Proof

Let $B$ be a set.

Existence. By Theorem 2.1, $B \subseteq B$. Since $B = B$, the subset $B$ of $B$ is not proper by Definition 2.5, so $B$ is an improper subset of itself.

Uniqueness. Let $A$ be any improper subset of $B$. Then $A \subseteq B$, and since $A$ is not proper, it is not the case that $A eq B$, i.e., $A = B$. So if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are both improper subsets of $B$, then $A_1 = B$ and $A_2 = B$. By the axiom of extension, $A_1$ and $A_2$ have exactly the same elements as $B$, and hence as each other, so $A_1 = A_2$. Thus $B$ is the one and only improper subset of $B$. $\square$

Exercise 2.1. Show that $A = B$ if and only if $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.

Solution

We prove both directions.

($\implies$) Suppose $A = B$. By Theorem 2.1, $A \subseteq A$. Replacing $A$ by $B$ on either side of this gives $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.

($\impliedby$) Suppose $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$. By Definition 2.2, $ orall x : (x \in A \implies x \in B)$ and $ orall x : (x \in B \implies x \in A)$. Together these give $ orall x : (x \in A \iff x \in B)$, so $A$ and $B$ have exactly the same elements. By the axiom of extension, $A = B$. $\square$

This is how equality of sets is proved in practice: show each set is a subset of the other.

Exercise 2.2. Construct any $5$ disjoint subsets of the integers and express them using set-builder notation, roster notation and plain English.

Solution

We read “disjoint” as pairwise disjoint: no two of the five sets share an element. Sort the integers by their remainder on division by $5$. For each $r \in \lbrace 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 brace$, let

\[A_r := \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 5 \mid (n - r) brace.\]

Written out:

  • $A_0 = \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 5 \mid n brace = \lbrace \dots, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, \dots brace$, the integers divisible by $5$.
  • $A_1 = \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 5 \mid (n - 1) brace = \lbrace \dots, -9, -4, 1, 6, 11, \dots brace$, the integers that leave remainder $1$ on division by $5$.
  • $A_2 = \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 5 \mid (n - 2) brace = \lbrace \dots, -8, -3, 2, 7, 12, \dots brace$, the integers that leave remainder $2$ on division by $5$.
  • $A_3 = \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 5 \mid (n - 3) brace = \lbrace \dots, -7, -2, 3, 8, 13, \dots brace$, the integers that leave remainder $3$ on division by $5$.
  • $A_4 = \lbrace n \in \mathbb{Z} : 5 \mid (n - 4) brace = \lbrace \dots, -6, -1, 4, 9, 14, \dots brace$, the integers that leave remainder $4$ on division by $5$.

Here the remainder is always taken in $\lbrace 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 brace$, so for example $-4 = 5 \cdot (-1) + 1$ leaves remainder $1$.

Pairwise disjointness. Suppose, for contradiction, that $n \in A_r$ and $n \in A_s$ for some $0 \le r \lt s \le 4$. Then $5 \mid (n - r)$ and $5 \mid (n - s)$, so $5$ divides their difference $(n - r) - (n - s) = s - r$. But $0 \lt s - r \le 4$, and no integer strictly between $0$ and $5$ is a multiple of $5$. This is a contradiction, so the five sets are pairwise disjoint. $\square$

Many other answers are equally valid. Five singletons such as $\lbrace 1 brace, \dots, \lbrace 5 brace$ technically work too, though that is a rather lazy way out.

Now for a theorem that a lot of textbooks would rather you didn’t hear about.

Theorem 2.4. There exists no universal set $U$ that contains all possible sets.

Proof

We will prove this by contradiction. Suppose such a set $U$ exists. By the axiom of specification with the predicate $P(x) :\iff x otin x$, we have the set $R := \lbrace x \in U : x otin x brace$. Since $U$ contains every set, $R$ contains every set that is not a member of itself, and nothing else. But Theorem 2.2 says no such set exists. This is a contradiction, so $U$ cannot be a set. $\square$

Remark 2.5. Many older texts, and some newer ones whose authors either do not know the subject or cannot do some basic research, suggest the existence of such a universal set. Theorem 2.4 settles that. What we can do instead is define something quite similar, relative to the sets we actually care about.

Definition 2.6. A set $U$ is a universal set for a given set $S$ if and only if every element of $S$ is a subset of $U$, i.e., $ orall X : (X \in S \implies X \subseteq U)$.

Remark 2.6. This definition presupposes that we already have a set of sets $S$, and the axiom of union guarantees that a universal set for it exists: the set containing every element of every $X \in S$ will do. In problems involving sets, we can intuitively imagine the universal set to be some set that simply includes all elements of the sets given to us. In principle, it can contain even more elements.

Example 2.9. For $S := \lbrace \lbrace 1, 2 brace, \lbrace 2, 3 brace, \lbrace 4, 5 brace brace$, the set $U = \lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 brace$ is a universal setFor the given set $S$, that is, not a universal set for everything..

Exercise 2.3. Verify that the claim made in Example 2.9 satisfies our definition of a universal set.

Solution

By Definition 2.6, we must check that every $X \in S$ satisfies $X \subseteq U$, where $U = \lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 brace$. The set $S$ has exactly three elements, so we check each in turn using Definition 2.2.

  • $X = \lbrace 1, 2 brace$: both $1 \in U$ and $2 \in U$, so $X \subseteq U$.
  • $X = \lbrace 2, 3 brace$: both $2 \in U$ and $3 \in U$, so $X \subseteq U$.
  • $X = \lbrace 4, 5 brace$: both $4 \in U$ and $5 \in U$, so $X \subseteq U$.

Hence $ orall X : (X \in S \implies X \subseteq U)$, and $U$ is a universal set for $S$. $\square$

Note that $U$ is not the only choice. The same check shows that $\lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 brace$, or $\mathbb{Z}$, is also a universal set for $S$. The set $\lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 brace$ is simply the smallest one, the one the axiom of union hands us.

So we now know what sets are, how to compare them, and which rules stop them from swallowing themselves whole. Next time, we start actually doing things with sets: unions, intersections, complements and differences. We will also cash in the promised consequences of the axiom of foundation. Strange axiom, isn’t it? Let’s see whether it earns its place.
entry.summary: What Sets Are, Why Naive Set Theory Breaks, and the ZFC Axioms That Fix It

entry.title: Why Physics Education?
entry.content:
My Formative Education

Now I am not gonna lie to you like every other wannabe and tell you about how I was a curious child and did yada yada yada when I was $-5$ or $-6$ (yes that is a minus lol) years old to impress you. On the contrary, like most kids in an Indian household, my curiosity was often curbed with ridiculous responses associated to either religion or tradition in a mutually non-exclusive manner. My early schooling days had a subpar mathematics education as well. So much so that by the third grade, I could recite the multiplication tables upto 20 like a champ but had no clue how to actually do multiplication. So how does a $7$ year old who cannot deal with numbers ends up in a mathematically rich area of study?

To answer the above, I need to talk about how my mathematics education developed. Around the end of my abysmal third grade, I had to switch both cities (from one hometown in Chennai to another in Kolkata) and schools. The level of education seemed to take a massive jump. With my memorization abilities I more or less got through the social studies topics and languages rather comfortably. Even the sciences to some degree, considering all the factual jargon they tend to throw at kids in elementary school around these parts.

entry.title: Welcome to my blog!
entry.content:
About this blog

Welcome to the first post on this blog! This website and the accompanying blog has been a long time coming but faced regular delays due to my procrastination. In this post, I aim to cover all the need-to-know stuff about this blog so that the visiting audience knows how to get around. The name of the blog itself is inspired by the educational philosophy of autodidactism. To paraphrase from Wikipedia,

Autodidactism is the practice of education without the guidance of teachers. Autodidacts are self-taught people who learn a subject through self-study. The process may involve, complement, or be an alternative to formal education. Formal education itself may have a hidden curriculum that requires self-study for the uninitiated.

With the above definition, I am hopeful that the reader has an inkling of what I am trying to achieve here. This blog’s primary function is as a resource for people interested in the beautiful interplay of the natural sciences and mathematics known to us as physics. Posts on this blog may range from a variety of online and open sourced educational content as recommendations to introductions to various topics and tools relevant to physics. Of course, this is not limited to just mathematical machinery, computational modelling or experimental details, but also philosophical, historical and social considerations. The blog will also occasionally feature educational content from colleagues and students of mine that fit the scope and vision of this endeavour. As a secondary function, the blog would also have a fair bit of my brand of whimsy and some of my travel diaries because we all need some humor and a nice backdrop to engage in productive endeavors lol. Anyhow, much of this website is still fairly empty, which include mainly my work prior to the summer of 2025.

Now, I do see the irony in an educator such as myself making a blog for autodidacts and the apparent contradiction of what autodidactism is, to my vocation. First, to address the apparent contradiction, this blog does not aim to teach but rather seeks to expose the uninitiated that may have landed here by chance or algorithmic design. The website in fact has a separate page that is dedicated to my teaching for my own students and those that may be too lost on their own to meet the autodidactic philosophy head-on. So, why does an educator such as myself endorse such a philosophy? It is a bit strange especially in this day and age with AI models running amok with hallucinated or biased content and social media algorithms that incentivise a confirmation bias. Educators such as myself should in fact be taking an active role to guide as opposed to leaving it all upto individual discretion! Well that is precisely the point of this blog. The hope is that the expositions here to both technical and social aspects through the lens of the physical sciences will inculcate critical thinking that re-inforces one’s individual discretion over the sway of heavily biased narratives.

That is about it with the introduction. The tags on the landing page of the blog can take you to an archive of posts that are tagged as such if your interests are narrow. For the complete beginner who wishes to study the physical sciences, a starter pack will soon be put up on this post.
